newsitem.title: USA: SEC alleges ponzi-scheme involving Arizona trusts.
newsitem.headline: SEC alleges ponzi-scheme involving Arizona trusts.

text.p: The Securities and Exchange Commission said Wednesday that it filed charges against three Arizona investment trusts, their trustees and the people who controlled them, alleging they bilked nearly 150 investors of millions of dollars in a ponzi-scheme.

In a civil complaint filed May 5 in U.S. District Court in Phoenix, the SEC filed charges against the three trusts, the trustees and their respective presidents, and a California attorney alleged to have been involved.
"People need to be very careful in their investments and need to think that if it sounds too good to be true, it probably isn't true," an SEC attorney handling the case said.

The SEC alleged that Southwest Income Trust, Advantage Income Trust, Investors Trading Trust and an Arizona corporation, PCI Ltd, collected at least $10.7 million from California and Arizona investors who were told they would receive payments monthly of one percent on the trust's alleged Treasury securities investments.

"Contrary to these representations, defendants operated a ponzi-like scheme that paid investors their one percent return per month from other investors' principal because the defendants' $3.4 million in losses trading Treasury securities made it impossible to pay investors their return from any other source," the agency said in its complaint.
Further, the agency alleged certain defendants misappropriated millions in investor funds for their personal benefit.

The individuals the SEC named in its case were: Anthony Ghirardello Marriott, a Pacific Palisades, Calif. attorney; Steven Robert Shoop, 45 of Phoenix, Donn Kenneth Phillips, 57 of Tucson; and Charles Douglas Brown, 58 of Apache Junction, Ariz.
Shoop and Brown could not be reached for comment.
Phillips told Reuters that the SEC is pursuing the wrong people in the case and that he, Shoop, Brown and the trusts have filed a suit against a Los Angeles law firm he accused of the wrong-doing.
"The tragedy is this (SEC) lawsuit really is inhibiting our ability to recover. We are not the ones that piddled away the money," Phillips said.
Ronald Nessim, an attorney representing Marriott, said he received the SEC's complaint yesterday. "Mr. Marriott is anxious to tell his account and will at the appropriate time," Nessim said.
